screens.title: Private Data Collections (PDCs) — Why and How
screens.narratorSegment: In many Fabric deployments you want most data visible to a channel, but sometimes a small group of participants needs to share sensitive content privately. Private Data Collections, or PDCs, solve that exact problem: they let a subset of organizations keep raw data off the main ledger while still recording a tamper-proof hash for audit. Today we'll walk through why PDCs matter, how private data travels from client to peer stores, and what trade-offs you must consider when designing collections. We'll use a supply chain scenario — a manufacturer and supplier sharing pricing terms while a logistics partner and regulator see only public order records — to ground the ideas. You will learn the roles of transient data, chaincode endorsement, the private data store, the gossip distribution mechanism, and the hash-on-chain pattern that preserves integrity without exposing content. Finally, we'll preview common use cases, configuration elements in collection_config. json, and key limitations such as gossip eventual consistency and query restrictions. After this lesson you should be able to decide when a PDC is the right privacy tool and how to reason about its security and operational complexity.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: PDCs keep raw private data accessible only to authorized peers while storing a hash on the main ledger to prove integrity and support auditability.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Private Data Collections
Private Data Collections
Keep raw data private to a subset of channel members while anchoring integrity publicly with a hash.
PDCs let you avoid creating separate channels for every private exchange. They provide selective visibility, a private data store on authorized peers, and a hash recorded on the main ledger for audit. We'll use real supply-chain examples to show where this matters and what to watch out for when designing policies and retention.
In this lesson
Architecture and flow of PDCs, examples, configuration, and operational trade-offs.
Transient Data
Where private values start — sent only to endorsers.
Hash On-Chain
Immutable proof a private write occurred without revealing content.
Private Data Store
Side database on authorized peers, e.g., CouchDB or LevelDB.
Interactive Concept Map
Manufacturer and Supplier exchange private terms via a PDC. The chaincode uses transient data and returns a hash that the orderer records. That hash preserves integrity while gossip shares the raw private payload only with authorized peers.
Coming up: detailed flow, config review, advantages and limits.

PDC transaction flow — how transient data, endorsement, hashing and gossip interact.
2

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the core privacy problem PDCs solve: selective confidentiality inside a channel. You will describe the architecture components — transient data, endorsing peers, the private data store, and the hash-on-chain pattern — and explain how they work together to keep raw data private while preserving auditability. You'll identify practical use cases such as supply chain finance, healthcare records, insurance claims, sealed bids, and trade-secret collaboration and explain why PDCs fit those scenarios. Finally, you will evaluate the trade-offs of choosing PDCs instead of creating more channels or relying on off-chain encryption and hashing. Each objective includes a short, practical skill: read a collection_config. json, reason about requiredPeerCount and blockToLive, and identify where gossip could introduce eventual consistency. This combination of conceptual and hands-on skills will help you design PDCs that balance confidentiality, integrity, and operational complexity.

requiredPeerCount & maxPeerCount

EndorsementPolicy
Must align with private collection membership so that endorsers see the transient values required to compute the hash.

screens.title: Why PDCs exist — the selective confidentiality problem
screens.narratorSegment: Private Data Collections exist because channels are too coarse-grained for many real-world privacy needs. Channels isolate transactions between groups, but they force you to create separate ledgers and governance per subgroup. That quickly becomes unmanageable when many combinations of participants need to exchange private information. PDCs solve a narrower, practical problem: allow a subset of organizations within a shared channel to keep specific data private while the channel still records the public history. For example, a manufacturer and supplier may share pricing agreements that logistics and regulators should not see, yet the entire channel still tracks shipment and order data. The core claim is simple: you want the efficiency of a single channel for shared state and the privacy of a separate store for sensitive fields. A common misconception is that PDCs hide everything from the network; they do not. The ordering service and non-member peers still see a cryptographic hash on the main ledger, which proves that a private write took place. That design gives auditability while protecting content. As a takeaway, think in terms of visibility and trust boundaries: PDCs are for data that must remain confidential only to a subset of channel members but still needs an immutable anchor for integrity checks.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: PDCs provide selective confidentiality for a subset of channel members without creating new channels.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Selective Confidentiality
Problem: channels are coarse
When many small groups need private exchanges, creating channels explodes governance overhead and duplicate chaincode.
Scenario
Manufacturer and supplier share pricing privately while the rest of the channel tracks shipments publicly.
Misconception
PDCs do not hide the fact a private write occurred; they store a hash publicly for integrity and audit.
How PDCs change the model
Share a channel for common state, but keep private fields in a side store for an authorized subset.
Record a cryptographic hash on the main ledger so integrity is auditable without revealing contents.
Key Takeaway

Use PDCs when you need confidentiality among a subset but still want a single shared ledger for the rest of the channel.

screens.title: PDC Architecture — private store and hash-on-chain
screens.narratorSegment: PDCs introduce two parallel storage concepts: the main channel ledger and a private data store on authorized peers. The main ledger continues to record ordered transactions and a hash of any private payload, while the private data store — typically a separate CouchDB or LevelDB instance — holds the raw private values only on authorized peers. The hash on the main ledger is crucial: it ties the private content to the immutable ledger state without exposing the content itself. This pattern preserves both confidentiality and integrity. Architecturally, the ordering service never receives raw private data; it only sees the transaction and the private-data hash. Gossip is the mechanism that moves raw private payloads peer-to-peer among collection members. A common pitfall is assuming the private store is replicated to all peers; it is not. Only the peers that are members of the collection receive and persist the raw data. Also remember that the private store is separate from world state and must be backed up and managed with retention rules mapped to blockToLive. The core operational insight is to treat the private store as a controlled sidecar to your main ledger that requires its own configuration and monitoring.

keyIdea.text: Main ledger stores hashes; authorized peers store raw data in a private data store. Ordering service never sees raw private data.

Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › PDC Architecture
Two storage layers
Main ledger: ordered transactions and private-data hashes. Private data store: raw private values only on collection members.
Main ledger (hashes)
Immutable record proving a private write occurred without exposing the payload.
Private data store
Separate DB on authorized peers; managed separately from world state and subject to retention policies.
Operational note
Back up private stores and configure blockToLive correctly. Treat them like sensitive sidecar databases.
Visual summary
Ordering service sees only hashes — never raw private data.
Gossip moves raw private payloads between authorized peers for storage.
Non-members keep only hashes and cannot read private content.

screens.title: End-to-end PDC transaction flow
screens.narratorSegment: A PDC transaction follows a precise, secure path. First, the client includes sensitive values as transient data in the proposal; transient data is never sent to the ordering service. Endorsing peers that belong to the collection receive the proposal and the transient payload, run chaincode that consumes that transient data, and compute the private-data hash. They return endorsements that include that hash but not the raw private values. The client assembles endorsements and sends the transaction — including the private-data hash — to the ordering service. The orderer creates a block containing the transaction and distributes it to all peers on the channel. Separately, a gossip-based private data distribution moves raw private payloads peer-to-peer only among collection members. When peers commit the block, members will have received the raw data and can persist it in the private data store; non-members will validate the transaction using the hash and store only the hash. A common mistake is assuming endorsers always persist private data automatically — gossip and correct collection membership must deliver the raw payload to members before commit. As a result, design your endorsement policies and requiredPeerCount to match availability and consistency needs.

keyIdea.title: Flow steps
keyIdea.text: Client -> transient data -> endorsers compute hash -> ordering sees hash -> gossip distributes raw data -> members persist raw data and hash.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Transaction Flow
Step-by-step
1
Client sends transient data in the proposal. It is not sent to the orderer.
2
Endorsers in the collection execute chaincode, process transient data, and compute a hash of the private payload.
3
Client assembles endorsements and sends the transaction with the private-data hash to the ordering service.
4
Orderer creates a block containing the transaction and distributes it to all peers; orderer never sees raw private data.
5
Gossip distributes raw private payloads only to collection members; members store raw data in the private data store and all peers store the hash.
Checklist & Pitfalls
  • Ensure endorsers for the collection actually receive transient data.
  • Set requiredPeerCount to support gossip availability.
  • Don't rely on the ordering service for confidentiality — it never sees raw data.
Key Takeaway

Design endorsement and gossip parameters to ensure private data reaches members before commit, otherwise you face missing private data at validation time.

screens.title: Gossip protocol — delivering raw private data
screens.narratorSegment: Gossip is the mechanism that moves raw private data between authorized peers in a PDC. Unlike the ordered block distribution, which reaches every peer with the transaction and hash, gossip runs peer-to-peer to ensure only collection members receive the raw payload. This design minimizes exposure, but it introduces operational complexity: gossip is eventually consistent, so private data distribution may lag the block delivery. If a member peer does not receive the private payload by the time it processes the block, it will record the transaction hash but be missing the raw values. Designers must therefore plan for requiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount to meet availability targets and consider how peers re-sync private data when they come back online. A frequent misconception is that gossip guarantees immediate delivery; it does not. Additionally, gossip requires proper network topology and connectivity among collection members. For critical data, you should tune the collection configuration and monitor private store replication to avoid scenarios where private reads fail because the raw payload was never received. The practical takeaway is to treat gossip as a secure but asynchronous delivery that needs explicit operational controls.

keyIdea.title: Gossip role
keyIdea.text: Gossip distributes raw private payloads peer-to-peer only to collection members; it is eventual, not immediate.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Gossip Distribution
Gossip: private payload delivery
Gossip sends raw private data peer-to-peer among collection members. It is separate from orderer block delivery.
Eventual consistency
Private data may arrive after the block. Plan for resyncs and monitoring to ensure availability.
Topology matters
Ensure network connectivity and peer membership allow gossip to reach required peers within SLAs.
Operational checklist
  • Monitor private store replication and gaps.
  • Tune requiredPeerCount to match expected redundancy.
  • Plan resync strategies for recovering peers.
Common mistake

Assuming gossip delivers instantly; in practice you must design for delayed delivery and recovery.

screens.title: Reading collection_config.json
screens.narratorSegment: The collection_config. json defines who participates in a PDC, how many peers should hold data, and how long private data lives. Key fields include name, policy, requiredPeerCount, maxPeerCount, blockToLive, memberOnlyRead, memberOnlyWrite, and endorsementPolicy. The policy string names the member MSPs who are allowed to access the collection; endorsementPolicy aligns endorsers with those members so they can compute hashes from transient data. requiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount inform gossip about replication targets and availability expectations. blockToLive sets retention in blocks, where zero means private data is not retained beyond commit for that collection. memberOnlyRead and memberOnlyWrite restrict read/write access to collection members. A practical example in the source shows Org1AndOrg2PrivateCollection with OR('Org1MSP. member', 'Org2MSP. member') and requiredPeerCount 1 which means at least one peer should hold the private data for basic availability. When reviewing configs, check that requiredPeerCount, endorsementPolicy, and membership align with your availability, audit, and governance goals. A common error is mismatching endorsementPolicy and the policy field which can prevent endorsers from seeing transient data needed to produce valid hashes. Reading collection_config.json means collection config fields determine membership, replication targets, retention, and endorsement alignment for private data.. In practical terms, members, policy, peer counts, and retention. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Configuration focus
keyIdea.text: Collection config fields determine membership, replication targets, retention, and endorsement alignment for private data.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › collection_config.json
Key fields explained
name: Identifier for the private collection used by chaincode.
policy: Member access policy, e.g., OR('Org1MSP.member', 'Org2MSP.member').
requiredPeerCount / maxPeerCount: Guidelines for gossip replication and availability.
blockToLive: Number of blocks private data is retained; 0 means not retained beyond commit.
Example excerpt
{
  "name": "Org1AndOrg2PrivateCollection",
  "policy": "OR('Org1MSP.member', 'Org2MSP.member')",
  "requiredPeerCount": 1,
  "maxPeerCount": 2,
  "blockToLive": 1000000,
  "memberOnlyRead": true,
  "memberOnlyWrite": true,
  "endorsementPolicy": {
    "signaturePolicy": "OR('Org1MSP.peer', 'Org2MSP.peer')"
  }
}
Check that endorsementPolicy matches the members allowed by policy so endorsers can see transient data and compute the hash.

screens.title: PDCs vs Channels vs Off-chain
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right privacy mechanism is a common design question. Channels give complete isolation by creating separate ledgers; they are straightforward but multiply governance, chaincode deployments, and complexity when many pairwise private relationships exist. Off-chain solutions can hide data entirely from the network by storing it externally and anchoring a hash on-chain, but they add complexity for availability, custody, and audit. PDCs sit between these extremes: they let you keep raw data private to a subset of channel members while anchoring integrity on the shared ledger. Use PDCs when you want a single channel for common state but need confidential fields shared among subgroups. They reduce channel proliferation and simplify governance compared to many channels, but they do add complexity to chaincode and client logic. A common mistake is assuming PDCs are a drop-in replacement for channels; they are best for selective confidentiality, not when you need full ledger isolation. The practical decision should weigh governance overhead, the number of private pairings, audit needs, and whether the ordering service must be prevented from seeing any evidence of the transaction — if complete secrecy from all channel participants is required, off-chain hashing may be more appropriate.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Use PDCs when you need selective privacy inside a channel; prefer channels for full ledger isolation or off-chain for complete secrecy from the ordering service.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Privacy Options
Channels
Complete isolation, separate ledger and governance; heavy when many combinations exist.
PDCs
Selective confidentiality inside a channel; hashes provide auditability while raw data stays with members.
Off-chain
Keep data external and anchor a hash on-chain; useful when you must hide data from all channel participants including orderer.
Quick guide
Choose channels when you need full ledger isolation and separate governance.
Choose PDCs when many subgroups need selective privacy but share common ledger state.
Choose off-chain hashing when the orderer or any peer must be denied knowledge of the transaction existence or content.
Consider operational complexity: PDCs add chaincode and client complexity; channels add governance overhead.

screens.title: Commitment and storage on peers
screens.narratorSegment: When a peer receives a block from the ordering service it runs validation steps and then commits state. For PDC transactions, all peers will validate the transaction and store the hash on the main ledger. Only peers that are members of the collection will have received the raw private payload via gossip; they persist the raw data in the private data store. Non-members record the hash but never see the raw values. The private data store is a separate database — often CouchDB or LevelDB — and it should be managed, backed up, and governed like any other sensitive store. One misconception is to treat the private data store as a copy of world state; it is not. It holds raw payloads tied to a collection and subject to blockToLive-based retention. If blockToLive expires, peers purge private entries per the configuration. Also, cross-collection queries are limited: only authorized peers can query their own private store, which makes analytics across private collections harder. The takeaway is to plan lifecycle policies and backups for private stores and to expect that only collection members can answer private queries.

keyIdea.title: Peer behaviour
keyIdea.text: All peers store the hash; only collection members store raw private data in a separate private data store with its own retention policy.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Peer Commit & Storage
Commit actions
All peers validate the transaction and store the private-data hash. Members persist raw data; non-members store only the hash.
Private store: Separate DB on members for raw values, subject to blockToLive retention.
Non-member view: Can validate the hash but cannot reconstruct the private payload.
Operational notes
  • Backup and protect private stores separately from world state.
  • Plan purges according to blockToLive to meet compliance.
  • Expect query restrictions for cross-collection analysis.
Key Takeaway

Private data storage has its own lifecycle and availability considerations separate from the main ledger; design backup and retention accordingly.

screens.title: Real-world use cases for PDCs
screens.narratorSegment: PDCs are valuable in scenarios where sensitive details must be restricted to a subset of participants while the broader channel retains shared state. A supply chain finance use case is common: a manufacturer and bank may share private loan terms or credit scores while other supply-chain participants see only public order details. In healthcare, patient records can be placed in a PDC shared between the patient, doctor and specific specialists while administrative records remain on the main ledger. Insurance claims benefit when insurers and claimants exchange claim details privately while regulators or auditors see only hashes or aggregated metrics. Bidding and auctions use PDCs to accept secret bids as private payloads and reveal only the final outcome publicly. Collaboration on trade secrets is another good fit: companies can keep proprietary designs or formulas in a PDC shared only with trusted partners. A misconception is trying to use PDCs to hide data from the ordering service; the orderer still sees hashes and evidence of the transaction. Use PDCs when you need confidentiality among a subset but also need an immutable public anchor for integrity and audit.

screens.title: Advantages of PDCs
screens.narratorSegment: PDCs offer several practical advantages. First, they provide granular confidentiality: you can share data with a subset of organizations without proliferating channels. That reduces governance and operational overhead when many private pairings are needed. Second, governance and chaincode management are simpler because you can reuse channel-level chaincode while restricting private fields via collections. Third, auditability is preserved because the hash of private data is recorded on the immutable ledger, giving verifiers the ability to detect tampering. Finally, data integrity is maintained: any change to private data would result in a hash mismatch against the public ledger entry. These strengths make PDCs attractive for collaborative networks that need both privacy and shared history. One thing to be careful about is assuming that PDCs remove the need for thoughtful governance: you still must define clear collection membership, endorsement rules, and retention. The immediate takeaway is that PDCs are a pragmatic middle ground: they reduce channel sprawl and maintain an auditable trail while enabling confidential sharing among limited participants. Advantages of PDCs means granular confidentiality, simplified governance, auditability through hashes, and preserved data integrity are the main advantages.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Advantages
Why choose PDCs?
Granular confidentiality for subsets of channel members without creating new channels.
Simplified governance: fewer ledgers, centralized policy for the channel with collection-level privacy.
Auditability: hash on the main ledger proves a private write occurred and supports integrity checks.
Practical note
PDCs give you the best of both worlds for many collaboration networks, but they require careful design of policies and operational monitoring for private stores and gossip replication.

screens.title: Limitations and operational considerations
screens.narratorSegment: PDCs are powerful but not a universal privacy silver bullet. First, they add complexity to chaincode and client applications because you must manage transient data, access checks, and collection-aware logic. Second, gossip introduces eventual consistency: private data delivery may lag, so peers could be missing raw payloads at validation time unless you design for that. Third, querying private data across collections or across non-member peers is limited; analysis that spans private collections can be difficult to implement. Finally, PDCs do not hide the existence of a private transaction from the ordering service or non-member peers — the hash is visible on the main ledger. When data must be completely hidden from all channel members, including the orderer, an off-chain solution with only a hash on-chain may be more appropriate. Operationally, you must plan backup and retention for private stores, align endorsementPolicy with membership, and monitor gossip health. The takeaway: use PDCs when their advantages outweigh the additional operational and development work, and choose alternatives when complete secrecy or simpler architecture is required. content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.7 › Limitations
Common limitations
Complexity: chaincode and clients must manage transient data and collection-aware logic.
Gossip eventual consistency: private data may not arrive before commit on some peers.
Query limitations: cross-collection queries are challenging and limited to authorized peers.
Not absolute secrecy: the hash on-chain reveals that a private transaction occurred.
Mitigations
  • Align endorsementPolicy and collection membership to ensure endorsers can compute hashes.
  • Set requiredPeerCount and monitor gossip health for availability.
  • Consider off-chain hashing when the orderer must not see any evidence of a transaction.

screens.title: Hands-on: review a collection_config.json
screens.narratorSegment: A practical way to learn PDCs is to review a real collection_config. json. Start by locating the collection name and verify it matches chaincode references. Next, read the policy expression to see which MSPs are included; the signaturePolicy under endorsementPolicy should match who must endorse private writes. Inspect requiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount: they influence how gossip will replicate private data and therefore affect availability. Check blockToLive to understand retention semantics — a value of zero means the collection does not retain private data beyond its commit. Confirm memberOnlyRead and memberOnlyWrite flags so that only authorized members can read or write private entries. A common check is to ensure that requiredPeerCount is not larger than maxPeerCount and that endorsementPolicy names peers that are actually members. After you identify these settings, ask yourself whether the policy and retention match compliance needs and whether network topology supports the expected gossip replication. This exercise builds practical intuition for how config values map to runtime behaviors. Hands-on: review a collection_config.json means practice mapping collection configuration fields to availability, privacy, and retention behaviours.. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts. First, a Private Data Collection is a Fabric feature that confines raw private data to a subset of organizations while recording a cryptographic hash on the main ledger for integrity and audit. Second, transient data is the mechanism clients use to send private payloads to endorsers; transient data is never sent to the ordering service. Third, the private data store is a side database on authorized peers where raw private values are persisted and managed separately from the main ledger. Keep these concepts in mind when designing privacy: the hash-on-chain pattern provides auditability without disclosure, gossip distributes raw payloads in an eventually consistent fashion, and collection configuration controls membership, replication, and retention. As a final question, ask yourself whether your privacy requirement needs selective confidentiality inside a channel or absolute secrecy from all channel participants — that determines whether a PDC, separate channel, or off-chain approach is right.

fullNarratorScript:
In many Fabric deployments you want most data visible to a channel, but sometimes a small group of participants needs to share sensitive content privately. Private Data Collections, or PDCs, solve that exact problem: they let a subset of organizations keep raw data off the main ledger while still recording a tamper-proof hash for audit. Today we'll walk through why PDCs matter, how private data travels from client to peer stores, and what trade-offs you must consider when designing collections. We'll use a supply chain scenario — a manufacturer and supplier sharing pricing terms while a logistics partner and regulator see only public order records — to ground the ideas. You will learn the roles of transient data, chaincode endorsement, the private data store, the gossip distribution mechanism, and the hash-on-chain pattern that preserves integrity without exposing content. Finally, we'll preview common use cases, configuration elements in collection_config. json, and key limitations such as gossip eventual consistency and query restrictions. After this lesson you should be able to decide when a PDC is the right privacy tool and how to reason about its security and operational complexity.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the core privacy problem PDCs solve: selective confidentiality inside a channel. You will describe the architecture components — transient data, endorsing peers, the private data store, and the hash-on-chain pattern — and explain how they work together to keep raw data private while preserving auditability. You'll identify practical use cases such as supply chain finance, healthcare records, insurance claims, sealed bids, and trade-secret collaboration and explain why PDCs fit those scenarios. Finally, you will evaluate the trade-offs of choosing PDCs instead of creating more channels or relying on off-chain encryption and hashing. Each objective includes a short, practical skill: read a collection_config. json, reason about requiredPeerCount and blockToLive, and identify where gossip could introduce eventual consistency. This combination of conceptual and hands-on skills will help you design PDCs that balance confidentiality, integrity, and operational complexity.

This second objectives screen focuses on practical capabilities you will practice. You will be able to examine a collection_config. json file and identify the collection name, membership policy, requiredPeerCount, maxPeerCount, blockToLive, and read/write restrictions. Understanding these fields matters because they directly affect gossip distribution, retention and who can see private entries. You will also learn to map endorsement rules for private writes to chaincode logic so that only authorized peers can process transient data and produce the private-data hash. Finally, you will be able to compare PDCs to alternatives like separate channels or off-chain storage and make a defensible choice based on factors such as governance overhead, audit requirements, and the need to hide data from all channel members. These practical skills let you both design and critique a PDC deployment for real operational networks.

Private Data Collections exist because channels are too coarse-grained for many real-world privacy needs. Channels isolate transactions between groups, but they force you to create separate ledgers and governance per subgroup. That quickly becomes unmanageable when many combinations of participants need to exchange private information. PDCs solve a narrower, practical problem: allow a subset of organizations within a shared channel to keep specific data private while the channel still records the public history. For example, a manufacturer and supplier may share pricing agreements that logistics and regulators should not see, yet the entire channel still tracks shipment and order data. The core claim is simple: you want the efficiency of a single channel for shared state and the privacy of a separate store for sensitive fields. A common misconception is that PDCs hide everything from the network; they do not. The ordering service and non-member peers still see a cryptographic hash on the main ledger, which proves that a private write took place. That design gives auditability while protecting content. As a takeaway, think in terms of visibility and trust boundaries: PDCs are for data that must remain confidential only to a subset of channel members but still needs an immutable anchor for integrity checks.

PDCs introduce two parallel storage concepts: the main channel ledger and a private data store on authorized peers. The main ledger continues to record ordered transactions and a hash of any private payload, while the private data store — typically a separate CouchDB or LevelDB instance — holds the raw private values only on authorized peers. The hash on the main ledger is crucial: it ties the private content to the immutable ledger state without exposing the content itself. This pattern preserves both confidentiality and integrity. Architecturally, the ordering service never receives raw private data; it only sees the transaction and the private-data hash. Gossip is the mechanism that moves raw private payloads peer-to-peer among collection members. A common pitfall is assuming the private store is replicated to all peers; it is not. Only the peers that are members of the collection receive and persist the raw data. Also remember that the private store is separate from world state and must be backed up and managed with retention rules mapped to blockToLive. The core operational insight is to treat the private store as a controlled sidecar to your main ledger that requires its own configuration and monitoring.

A PDC transaction follows a precise, secure path. First, the client includes sensitive values as transient data in the proposal; transient data is never sent to the ordering service. Endorsing peers that belong to the collection receive the proposal and the transient payload, run chaincode that consumes that transient data, and compute the private-data hash. They return endorsements that include that hash but not the raw private values. The client assembles endorsements and sends the transaction — including the private-data hash — to the ordering service. The orderer creates a block containing the transaction and distributes it to all peers on the channel. Separately, a gossip-based private data distribution moves raw private payloads peer-to-peer only among collection members. When peers commit the block, members will have received the raw data and can persist it in the private data store; non-members will validate the transaction using the hash and store only the hash. A common mistake is assuming endorsers always persist private data automatically — gossip and correct collection membership must deliver the raw payload to members before commit. As a result, design your endorsement policies and requiredPeerCount to match availability and consistency needs.

Gossip is the mechanism that moves raw private data between authorized peers in a PDC. Unlike the ordered block distribution, which reaches every peer with the transaction and hash, gossip runs peer-to-peer to ensure only collection members receive the raw payload. This design minimizes exposure, but it introduces operational complexity: gossip is eventually consistent, so private data distribution may lag the block delivery. If a member peer does not receive the private payload by the time it processes the block, it will record the transaction hash but be missing the raw values. Designers must therefore plan for requiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount to meet availability targets and consider how peers re-sync private data when they come back online. A frequent misconception is that gossip guarantees immediate delivery; it does not. Additionally, gossip requires proper network topology and connectivity among collection members. For critical data, you should tune the collection configuration and monitor private store replication to avoid scenarios where private reads fail because the raw payload was never received. The practical takeaway is to treat gossip as a secure but asynchronous delivery that needs explicit operational controls.

The collection_config. json defines who participates in a PDC, how many peers should hold data, and how long private data lives. Key fields include name, policy, requiredPeerCount, maxPeerCount, blockToLive, memberOnlyRead, memberOnlyWrite, and endorsementPolicy. The policy string names the member MSPs who are allowed to access the collection; endorsementPolicy aligns endorsers with those members so they can compute hashes from transient data. requiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount inform gossip about replication targets and availability expectations. blockToLive sets retention in blocks, where zero means private data is not retained beyond commit for that collection. memberOnlyRead and memberOnlyWrite restrict read/write access to collection members. A practical example in the source shows Org1AndOrg2PrivateCollection with OR('Org1MSP. member', 'Org2MSP. member') and requiredPeerCount 1 which means at least one peer should hold the private data for basic availability. When reviewing configs, check that requiredPeerCount, endorsementPolicy, and membership align with your availability, audit, and governance goals. A common error is mismatching endorsementPolicy and the policy field which can prevent endorsers from seeing transient data needed to produce valid hashes. Reading collection_config.json means collection config fields determine membership, replication targets, retention, and endorsement alignment for private data.. In practical terms, members, policy, peer counts, and retention. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing the right privacy mechanism is a common design question. Channels give complete isolation by creating separate ledgers; they are straightforward but multiply governance, chaincode deployments, and complexity when many pairwise private relationships exist. Off-chain solutions can hide data entirely from the network by storing it externally and anchoring a hash on-chain, but they add complexity for availability, custody, and audit. PDCs sit between these extremes: they let you keep raw data private to a subset of channel members while anchoring integrity on the shared ledger. Use PDCs when you want a single channel for common state but need confidential fields shared among subgroups. They reduce channel proliferation and simplify governance compared to many channels, but they do add complexity to chaincode and client logic. A common mistake is assuming PDCs are a drop-in replacement for channels; they are best for selective confidentiality, not when you need full ledger isolation. The practical decision should weigh governance overhead, the number of private pairings, audit needs, and whether the ordering service must be prevented from seeing any evidence of the transaction — if complete secrecy from all channel participants is required, off-chain hashing may be more appropriate.

When a peer receives a block from the ordering service it runs validation steps and then commits state. For PDC transactions, all peers will validate the transaction and store the hash on the main ledger. Only peers that are members of the collection will have received the raw private payload via gossip; they persist the raw data in the private data store. Non-members record the hash but never see the raw values. The private data store is a separate database — often CouchDB or LevelDB — and it should be managed, backed up, and governed like any other sensitive store. One misconception is to treat the private data store as a copy of world state; it is not. It holds raw payloads tied to a collection and subject to blockToLive-based retention. If blockToLive expires, peers purge private entries per the configuration. Also, cross-collection queries are limited: only authorized peers can query their own private store, which makes analytics across private collections harder. The takeaway is to plan lifecycle policies and backups for private stores and to expect that only collection members can answer private queries.

A practical way to learn PDCs is to review a real collection_config. json. Start by locating the collection name and verify it matches chaincode references. Next, read the policy expression to see which MSPs are included; the signaturePolicy under endorsementPolicy should match who must endorse private writes. Inspect requiredPeerCount and maxPeerCount: they influence how gossip will replicate private data and therefore affect availability. Check blockToLive to understand retention semantics — a value of zero means the collection does not retain private data beyond its commit. Confirm memberOnlyRead and memberOnlyWrite flags so that only authorized members can read or write private entries. A common check is to ensure that requiredPeerCount is not larger than maxPeerCount and that endorsementPolicy names peers that are actually members. After you identify these settings, ask yourself whether the policy and retention match compliance needs and whether network topology supports the expected gossip replication. Let's summarize the essential concepts. First, a Private Data Collection is a Fabric feature that confines raw private data to a subset of organizations while recording a cryptographic hash on the main ledger for integrity and audit. Second, transient data is the mechanism clients use to send private payloads to endorsers; transient data is never sent to the ordering service. Third, the private data store is a side database on authorized peers where raw private values are persisted and managed separately from the main ledger. Keep these concepts in mind when designing privacy: the hash-on-chain pattern provides auditability without disclosure, gossip distributes raw payloads in an eventually consistent fashion, and collection configuration controls membership, replication, and retention. As a final question, ask yourself whether your privacy requirement needs selective confidentiality inside a channel or absolute secrecy from all channel participants — that determines whether a PDC, separate channel, or off-chain approach is right.

Keep this quick reference in mind as you design PDCs. A private-data hash is the cryptographic fingerprint written to the main ledger that lets anyone verify integrity without seeing content. The gossip protocol is the secure peer-to-peer channel that distributes raw private data only to collection members; it is eventual, not instantaneous. Collection configuration defines members, endorsement requirements, replication targets, and retention; these fields map directly to operational behaviours. When in doubt, validate that endorsementPolicy and policy line up and that requiredPeerCount reflects your desired redundancy. These short reminders will help you both read existing PDC setups and design new ones that meet confidentiality, availability and audit requirements.
